title: Math: Count Primes (Sieve of Eratosthenes)
oneLiner: Count the primes below n by crossing out multiples instead of testing each number on its own.
keyTakeaway: Testing every number for primality costs about n times the square root of n. The Sieve of Eratosthenes flips it round: for each prime p with p * p < n, cross out p * p, p * p + p, and so on. Whatever survives is prime. Total work is O(n log log n), which is practically linear, for O(n) memory.
explanation:
Return how many prime numbers are strictly less than n. A prime is a whole number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and so on. 1 is not prime, and neither is 0. For n = 10 the answer is 4 (2, 3, 5, 7).

The direct approach checks each k below n by trying divisors from 2 up to the square root of k (if k = a * b, one of the two is at most the square root, so you never need to look further). That is roughly n * sqrt(n) work: about a billion steps for n = 2,000,000, too slow here.

The Sieve of Eratosthenes works the other way. Make a boolean array isPrime[0..n-1], all true except 0 and 1. Walk p = 2, 3, 4, ... while p * p < n. If isPrime[p] is still true, p is prime, so cross out its multiples: p * p, p * p + p, p * p + 2p, up to n - 1. Start at p * p because every smaller multiple, such as 2p or 3p, has a smaller prime factor and was already crossed out. When the loop ends, count the trues.

Why O(n log log n)? Prime p crosses out about n / p numbers, and the sum of 1 / p over primes up to n grows like log log n, which is under 4 for any n you'll meet. Memory is one flag per number, O(n). In C# a bool[] costs a byte per flag; in Python a bytearray is far smaller and faster than a list of bools, and slice assignment (flags[p*p::p] = bytes(...)) crosses out a whole run in one step.

Overflow: in C#, 46,341 * 46,341 is past int.MaxValue (2,147,483,647), so the int product wraps round to a negative number. For n above 2,147,395,600 the test p * p < n would stay true at p = 46,341 and the inner loop would index a negative position. The tests here stop at 2,000,000, but (long)p * p < n, or p <= n / p, is the habit to build. Python ints never overflow, so p * p is always exact there.

The visualization sieves the numbers below 30.

recognitionSignals: "Count / list all primes up to n", or many primality questions about numbers in one known range.
n is large (around a million) and checking each number separately is too slow.
The same divisibility facts are needed for many numbers at once: precompute them in one table.
gotchas: "Less than n" excludes n itself: n = 2 has no primes below it, and n = 0 or 1 must return 0 without indexing past the array.
Start crossing out at p * p, and only for p with p * p < n; starting at 2p is still correct but does extra work.
In C#, p * p can overflow int for large p; compare (long)p * p or use p <= n / p.
confusableWith: Prime factorisation of ONE number only needs trial division up to its square root; the sieve pays off when you need many numbers' answers.
Prefix Sums: once you have the sieve, a prefix count array answers "how many primes in [a, b]?" in O(1) per query.

complexity.note: Each prime p crosses out about n / p numbers, and the sum of 1 / p over primes up to n grows like log log n. The sieve stores one flag per number below n.
